decisions.title: Onboarding question sets are driven by CoverBase configuration, not hard-coded in the Hazel application
decisions.statement: The questions asked during institution onboarding are defined in CoverBase and rendered from whatever CoverBase holds — if CoverBase is configured with ten questions, ten appear. Nothing is hard-coded in the Hazel application, so the question set can change over time without a code change. This answers Aaron McWilliams' request that the build assume the list of questions will change.

evidence.excerpt: just keep that in mind that the list of questions may change here or there and we want to build with that.

These questions will come from... cover base and it will be whatever we define it in cover base. So if cover base has 10, it will pop up from there. We will not be hard coding anything in our application.
Ohh, okay. Oh, well, I like that. No, that's good. That's perfect, Ed.

decisions.confidence_note: Shantanu Wadodkar states it as the way the build already works and Aaron McWilliams endorses it outright, so the intent is unambiguous. What is not established is feasibility: seconds later Shantanu Wadodkar says "We will let you know if that is possible in cover base" and that the team is still reading the CoverBase API documentation (CAND-Q-006). The decision is therefore a design commitment made before the integration was proven.

decisions.statement: CoverBase requires an institution profile — including a contacts answer — before it will run. The contacts section is not presented to the applicant as a question: the workflow already knows who the user is from earlier steps, and that information is auto-populated into the CoverBase answer instead. The wider principle Shantanu Wadodkar states is that nothing is asked twice when CoverBase or an earlier step already holds it.

The substance is clear. Two attributes are not: which earlier step supplies the contact data is never named, and the discussion runs against a screen share, so which fields make up "the contacts" section cannot be recovered from the source.

The presentation of the optional note is hedged ("maybe just some kind of note") and left to the build team. The required document is again referred to only as "the required document" against a screen share, which is the same gap registry Q-012 records. "Wolfsburg"/"Wolfberg" in the source is Wolfsberg.

decisions.title: Eligibility screening runs on a public pre-login page; no account and no CoverBase data until it passes
decisions.statement: Onboarding splits into two steps. Step one is a public inquiry page requiring no user ID or password, where an applicant enters institution details including an FDIC certificate number and an e-mail address. That data is stored in Hazel only and never reaches CoverBase. Hazel then validates the institution — an FDIC certificate number check performed on the back end, plus the RAFA report — and if both pass, an e-mail invites the applicant to create a user ID and password. Only in step two, after that gate, does the applicant answer onboarding questions and does data flow into CoverBase.

evidence.excerpt: So on a public side, public side in the Saenz without person getting a secured user ID and password, he can put his details. The details will be entered on a public inquiry page.
We get that detail, we store it in Hazel somewhere, not going to be in a cover base.
So the step number one has nothing to do with cover base. Moment that is approved, we will jump onto the step #2 and this data will go into the cover base now.
Yeah, we do have it. We will be doing this at the back end. We'll clarify, we'll validate if it is there or not, if it is correct or not.
those are the two main things here in step one we're looking forward. And if they both, you know, pass the criteria as we said, then we'll move forward automatically.

decisions.confidence_note: Shantanu Wadodkar presents the two-step workflow explicitly for validation — "let's put it on a paper so that we understand. and then we can validate is it right or wrong" — rather than as a settled call. The meeting then worked through it in detail without anyone disputing the shape, and Aaron McWilliams closes step one by naming its two gate criteria and confirming automatic progression. What remains unfixed is which institution identifier the public page collects (CAND-Q-003) and what happens to applicants who do not clear the gate (CAND-Q-002).

decisions.title: For MVP a RAFA score of 1 or 2 admits automatically; anything else goes to human review
decisions.statement: The eligibility gate is scored from the RAFA report. For MVP, a score of one or two is an automatic yes and the applicant continues without any human involvement. Any other score routes to human review. The thresholds are to be made configurable later, but the simple two-state rule is what is built now. The underlying intent Shawn Main gives is that Hazel is not trying to be exclusive: any insured, regulated institution is admitted, and what varies by risk is the transaction capability they get, not whether they are let in.

Note for the librarian that this sits alongside, not against, DEC-014: DEC-014 governs the CoverBase residual risk score later in due diligence, this governs the RAFA pre-screen at the gate. "RAPA", "Rafa", "raffle" and "offer report" in the source are all RAFA.

The applicant-facing UI on the public page says only that Hazel will reach out in a couple of days. The e-mail send is automated even where the underlying admit/decline judgement is a human one.

decisions.title: The RAFA report runs inside Hazel as part of HOP, not by calling Vantage
decisions.statement: Hazel runs its own version of the RAFA report on its own infrastructure, as part of HOP. The RAFA architecture currently living in Vantage's Databricks is reproduced inside Hazel rather than reached across the network, so there are no API calls out of Hazel to Vantage for the score. Shawn Main notes this does not preclude partitioning the engine off later — it need not be fully integrated, but it runs on the same internal infrastructure and can be treated as part of HOP.

decisions.title: No separate FDIC system is called at the gate; the UBPR data Hazel holds is the source
decisions.statement: Institution verification at the eligibility gate does not call out to a separate FDIC system. The UBPR data behind the RAFA report tracks effectively the same information via the RSSD ID, so Hazel uses the RAFA report for now and expands the check later if needed. Shawn Main's stated exception is that the FDIC may hold slightly different data for a bank that has not filed a report.

decisions.confidence_note: Shawn Main rules it out with a reason and nobody disputes that part. It bears directly on registry Q-014, which asks whether the FDIC number can be validated against a public FDIC API — this says no external call is made at all. Two things stop it being high confidence: Pallavi Bichpuriya said minutes earlier that an FDIC certificate number check is already implemented on the back end without stating what it calls, and Shantanu Wadodkar closes the topic by defending the FDIC number as the field to collect because banks know it, then defers the whole identifier question (CAND-Q-003). "UVPR" is UBPR; "raffle report" is the RAFA report.

decisions.statement: The NDA is not a CoverBase requirement — it is one of the steps that precedes CoverBase entirely. Once an applicant signs in to the HOP portal, the NDA is the first thing they do, before the basic inquiry form and the institution profile. Sequencing it first keeps the institution profile and all the onboarding questions together as one block inside CoverBase.

Alongside it sits threshold logic that decides, from the RAFA score, whether to send the continue e-mail immediately or route to that queue.

final_takeaways: Nothing in this delta is authoritative. Every item is a candidate for librarian review.
10 candidate decisions, 6 open questions, 7 action items, 8 items deliberately not promoted.

CAND-Q-001 is the item to read first: Aaron McWilliams says he is still waiting to learn whether banks that skip the Wolfsberg upload are asked other questions. DEC-009 was approved two days ago recording that they are not. Either DEC-009 was decided ahead of the confirmation it depends on, or Aaron McWilliams is not aware of it — the librarian should resolve which before the answer arrives.

CAND-DEC-005 and CAND-DEC-007 are the two high-confidence records, both called by Shawn Main: RAFA one-or-two admits automatically for MVP with everything else to human review, and RAFA runs entirely inside Hazel with no calls out to Vantage.

CAND-DEC-005 sits alongside DEC-014 rather than against it — DEC-014 governs the CoverBase residual risk score in due diligence, this governs the RAFA pre-screen at the gate. They should not be merged, but a reader of the registry will need the distinction spelled out.

CAND-DEC-008 bears on registry Q-014, which asks whether the FDIC number can be validated against a public FDIC API. Shawn Main's answer is that no external FDIC call is made at all — but Shantanu Wadodkar then defended keeping the FDIC number as the field collected, so CAND-Q-003 must settle before Q-014 can be closed.

CAND-DEC-004 describes a public, pre-authentication inquiry page that stores institution data in Hazel before any account exists. No decision covers what is retained for applicants who are declined, and the search-box exchange shows the team is already alive to the abuse surface — worth a look alongside registry Q-008.
blocking_reasons: All candidates require librarian approval before any record or ticket can be created.
CAND-Q-001 puts DEC-009 in question. Until it is answered, the Wolfsberg fallback behaviour has one approved record and one contradicting statement from the person who owns the answer.
